stem: A parent asks for diphenoxylate/atropine for a 4-year-old with watery diarrhea and no fever. What is the best answer?

options.A: Yes, at half the adult dose
options.B: Yes; the atropine prevents any overdose
options.C: Use loperamide instead at the adult dose
options.D: No: under 6 it can depress breathing
options.E: Yes, if limited to 2 days

why: Diphenoxylate/atropine is contraindicated under 6 years (respiratory depression and anticholinergic toxicity, especially in children). The atropine is a subtherapeutic dose to deter misuse.

whys.A: Contraindicated under 6 years, not dose-adjusted.
whys.B: Subtherapeutic atropine discourages misuse; it doesn't prevent toxicity.
whys.C: Loperamide is contraindicated under 2 and dosing is not adult.
whys.E: Duration does not lift the age contraindication.

takeaway: Lomotil: not under 6; atropine deters abuse.
discriminator: Know why the atropine is there — and that it is not a safety net.

stem: A 19-year-old receives IV metoclopramide in the ED for vomiting. Two hours later her neck twists to one side and her eyes deviate upward. What is happening and what treats it?

options.A: Tardive dyskinesia; stop and wait months
options.B: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; give dantrolene
options.C: Acute dystonia; give diphenhydramine or benztropine
options.D: A focal seizure; give diazepam
options.E: Anticholinergic toxicity; give physostigmine

why: D2 blockade by metoclopramide (and prochlorperazine) can cause acute dystonia within hours to days; diphenhydramine or benztropine reverses it. Tardive dyskinesia is the long-term boxed warning.

whys.A: Tardive dyskinesia appears after long-term use.
whys.B: No fever or rigidity crisis described; this is dystonia.
whys.D: Sustained posturing with eye deviation after a D2 blocker is dystonia.
whys.E: Metoclopramide is a D2 blocker, not an anticholinergic.

takeaway: Early dystonia (hours) vs. tardive dyskinesia (months) — both from D2 blockade.
discriminator: Time course separates the two movement disorders.

stem: Before azathioprine is started for Crohn disease, genetic testing shows very low TPMT activity. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: High myelosuppression risk at standard doses
options.B: Faster onset of remission within days
options.C: No change, since TPMT affects only allopurinol
options.D: Lower drug levels, so a higher dose is needed
options.E: Higher risk of acute pancreatitis only

why: Test TPMT and NUDT15 before thiopurines: low activity raises myelosuppression risk. Monitor CBC and liver tests; onset takes weeks to months — a Unit 1 pharmacogenomics principle.

whys.C: TPMT metabolizes thiopurines.
whys.D: Low TPMT raises active metabolite levels.
whys.E: The taught TPMT risk is bone marrow suppression.

takeaway: Low TPMT/NUDT15 → myelosuppression with azathioprine or 6-MP.
discriminator: Poor metabolizer → more active drug → more toxicity.

stem: A patient with stage 4 CKD has taken Milk of Magnesia daily for months for heartburn and constipation. She now has hypotension, absent deep-tendon reflexes and slow breathing. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Hypomagnesemia from chronic acid suppression
options.B: Hypermagnesemia from magnesium accumulating in CKD
options.C: Hypokalemia from chronic laxative use
options.D: Aluminum accumulation causing encephalopathy
options.E: Milk-alkali syndrome from excess calcium

why: Magnesium is renally cleared. In severe renal impairment it accumulates: hypotension, absent reflexes, respiratory depression and cardiac arrest. Severe renal impairment is a contraindication.

whys.A: PPIs lower magnesium; this patient has too much.
whys.C: Stimulant laxatives cause hypokalemia; this pattern is magnesium toxicity.
whys.D: Aluminum hydroxide, not magnesium, causes that.
whys.E: That is calcium carbonate.

takeaway: Mg antacid/laxative + CKD → hypermagnesemia (reflexes vanish first).
discriminator: Each antacid's CKD problem: Mg → hypermagnesemia; Al → osteomalacia/encephalopathy; Ca → milk-alkali.

stem: An 86-year-old with Alzheimer dementia in a nursing home has nausea. Which antiemetic carries a boxed warning that applies directly to her?

options.A: Meclizine
options.B: Aprepitant
options.C: Dexamethasone
options.D: Prochlorperazine
options.E: Ondansetron

why: Prochlorperazine (a phenothiazine D2 blocker) carries a boxed warning for dementia-related psychosis, plus dystonia, TD, NMS, QT prolongation and sedation.

whys.A: Anticholinergic caution in older adults; no boxed warning.
whys.C: Steroid risks; no dementia boxed warning.
whys.E: QT risk, but no dementia boxed warning.

takeaway: Prochlorperazine boxed warning: dementia-related psychosis.
discriminator: Older adult + dementia is a filter that removes the phenothiazine.

stem: A patient with mild ulcerative colitis has taken mesalamine 4.8 g daily for 6 months. His creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.6 mg/dL with no other cause. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Expected prerenal change from diarrhea
options.B: Steroid-induced kidney injury
options.C: Acute intolerance syndrome
options.D: Thiopurine-related hepatotoxicity
options.E: Interstitial nephritis from the 5-ASA agent

why: Mesalamine (5-ASA) is first-line for mild UC; its key toxicity is interstitial nephritis, so creatinine is monitored. Acute intolerance syndrome mimics a flare.

whys.A: Mild disease, no other cause; mesalamine needs creatinine monitoring.
whys.C: That causes cramps and bloody diarrhea, not creatinine rise.
whys.D: He is not on a thiopurine; the kidney is affected.

takeaway: Mesalamine: monitor creatinine (interstitial nephritis).
discriminator: Separate the kidney toxicity from the flare-like intolerance syndrome.

stem: A grandmother asks if she can give her 18-month-old grandson some of her linaclotide for constipation. What is the key safety point?

options.A: Boxed warning: fatal dehydration under age 2
options.B: It is safe if mixed with plenty of fluid
options.C: It is safe at one quarter of the adult capsule dose
options.D: It only causes mild diarrhea in children
options.E: It is safe because it is not absorbed

why: Linaclotide (a secretagogue) has a boxed warning against use in children under 2 years — severe dehydration and deaths; also mechanical GI obstruction is a contraindication.

whys.B: Fluid does not remove the boxed warning.
whys.C: Contraindicated under 2 years (boxed warning).
whys.D: Deaths from dehydration occurred in young children.
whys.E: Local action still caused fatal dehydration.

takeaway: Linaclotide: boxed warning under 2 years.
discriminator: Secretagogues pull fluid into the gut — dangerous in small children.
src: L06 S4; S5; S61; SG U3-R9

stem: A 66-year-old had a coronary stent placed 2 months ago and takes clopidogrel and warfarin. He now has erosive GERD that needs daily acid suppression for 8 weeks. Which choice best fits?

options.A: Esomeprazole 40 mg daily before breakfast
options.B: Calcium carbonate 1,000 mg after each meal
options.C: Omeprazole 20 mg daily before breakfast
options.D: Cimetidine 400 mg twice daily with meals
options.E: Pantoprazole 40 mg daily before a meal

why: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19, which omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit. Pantoprazole has fewer CYP interactions and still gives full PPI potency; cimetidine would also raise warfarin levels.

whys.A: Same CYP2C19 concern as omeprazole.
whys.B: Neutralizes acid briefly; does not heal erosive GERD.
whys.C: Inhibits CYP2C19 and can blunt clopidogrel activation.
whys.D: Strong CYP inhibitor that raises warfarin levels.

takeaway: Clopidogrel (or several CYP-sensitive drugs) + PPI need → pantoprazole.
discriminator: Two drugs, two CYP traps: CYP2C19 (omeprazole) and broad CYP inhibition (cimetidine).

stem: A 70-year-old on metformin and long-term omeprazole has macrocytic anemia. Folic acid alone is started; the anemia improves, but numbness in her feet worsens. What happened?

options.A: Folic acid toxicity caused neuropathy
options.B: Iron deficiency developed on folate
options.C: B12 deficiency masked by the folate
options.D: The PPI caused hypomagnesemia neuropathy
options.E: Metformin directly damages peripheral nerves

why: PPIs and metformin impair B12 absorption. Folate alone can correct the anemia while neurologic damage from B12 deficiency progresses and can become irreversible. Check and replace B12.

whys.A: Folic acid has low toxicity; B12 deficiency drives the nerve damage.
whys.B: Iron deficiency is microcytic, not this picture.
whys.D: The pattern is B12 deficiency.
whys.E: Metformin impairs B12 absorption.

takeaway: Long-term PPI or metformin → check B12; never folate alone.
discriminator: A fixed blood count does not mean the cause is fixed.

stem: A patient on simvastatin with no drug allergies and no prior macrolide use is about to start clarithromycin triple therapy for H. pylori. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: No interaction, since clarithromycin affects only warfarin
options.B: Lower simvastatin levels from CYP3A4 induction
options.C: Disulfiram-like reaction with the statin
options.D: Contraindicated: CYP3A4 inhibition raises the statin
options.E: Reduced clarithromycin effect from simvastatin

why: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitor; co-use with simvastatin, lovastatin or ergotamine is contraindicated. It also prolongs QT. An inhibitor raises the victim drug's level and toxicity.

whys.A: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitor.
whys.C: That is metronidazole with alcohol.
whys.E: The statin is the victim drug, not the perpetrator.

takeaway: Clarithromycin + simvastatin/lovastatin/ergotamine = contraindicated (CYP3A4).
discriminator: Perpetrator vs. victim: the inhibitor raises the other drug's level (Unit 1).

stem: A patient with Crohn disease in remission on azathioprine now has recurrent gout and needs urate-lowering therapy. Which plan is safest?

options.A: Stop azathioprine permanently before any gout drug
options.B: Febuxostat at the usual starting dose
options.C: Add colchicine daily instead of urate-lowering therapy
options.D: Allopurinol plus a major azathioprine dose cut
options.E: Allopurinol at full dose with no azathioprine change

why: Xanthine oxidase metabolizes thiopurines. Allopurinol requires a major thiopurine dose cut (about two-thirds to three-quarters) with CBC monitoring; febuxostat use with azathioprine is contraindicated.

whys.A: Dose reduction with monitoring is the taught approach.
whys.C: Prophylaxis does not lower urate.
whys.E: Allopurinol blocks thiopurine metabolism → myelosuppression.

takeaway: Thiopurine + allopurinol → cut the thiopurine dose; + febuxostat → contraindicated.
discriminator: A Unit 2 drug and a Unit 3 drug meeting at xanthine oxidase.

stem: An 81-year-old with an esophageal stricture and trouble swallowing has chronic constipation. Which option is the best fit?

options.A: Methylcellulose 2 g in water
options.B: Psyllium 3.4 g with a full glass of water
options.C: Senna 17.2 mg nightly long term
options.D: Lactulose 30–45 mL four times daily
options.E: Polyethylene glycol 3350, 17 g in fluid daily

why: Bulk-forming laxatives (psyllium, methylcellulose) can obstruct the esophagus or intestine without enough fluid and are contraindicated with dysphagia. PEG 3350 is an osmotic agent mixed into fluid.

whys.A: Bulk-formers are avoided with dysphagia.
whys.B: Dysphagia is a contraindication; risk of esophageal obstruction.
whys.C: Chronic use: hypokalemia, dependence; not the best fit.
whys.D: That is the hepatic encephalopathy dose.

takeaway: Dysphagia → avoid bulk-formers; choose an osmotic (PEG).
discriminator: Patient factor first, then the class.

stem: A 52-year-old with diabetic gastroparesis also has a seizure disorder controlled on medication. Which statement about metoclopramide is correct for her?

options.A: Contraindicated because of the seizure disorder
options.B: It is safe at 10 mg before meals and at bedtime only
options.C: It is safe if limited to 12 weeks
options.D: It is fine if she has never had dystonia
options.E: It is preferred because it is prokinetic

why: Metoclopramide is contraindicated with GI obstruction/perforation/bleeding, pheochromocytoma, seizure disorder and a history of tardive dyskinesia. The 12-week limit is for TD risk.

whys.B: Dose does not remove the contraindication.
whys.C: The 12-week limit addresses tardive dyskinesia, not seizures.
whys.D: History of TD is a contraindication; seizures are too.
whys.E: Prokinetic, but a seizure disorder is a contraindication.

takeaway: Metoclopramide contraindications: obstruction, pheochromocytoma, seizures, prior TD.
discriminator: The 12-week rule is a safety limit, not a pass for other contraindications.

stem: A patient finished 14 days of H. pylori therapy 3 weeks ago and still takes omeprazole daily for reflux. He wants proof of cure this week. What is the best plan?

options.A: Stool antigen test now; a PPI does not matter
options.B: No test is needed if symptoms have resolved
options.C: Stop the PPI now and test in at least 2 weeks
options.D: Urea breath test this week while on the PPI
options.E: Repeat the full course empirically

why: Test of cure (urea breath test or stool antigen) at least 4 weeks after therapy with the PPI held for 2 weeks. Stopping now satisfies both: 5+ weeks after therapy and 2 weeks off the PPI.

whys.A: PPIs suppress the organism and cause false negatives.
whys.D: PPIs cause false negatives; too soon after therapy.
whys.E: Confirm before re-treating.

takeaway: Test of cure: ≥ 4 weeks after therapy, PPI off ≥ 2 weeks.
discriminator: Two clocks run at once — time since therapy and time off the PPI.

stem: A 35-year-old with congenital long QT syndrome starts highly emetogenic chemotherapy. Which antiemetic is contraindicated for her?

options.A: Meclizine
options.B: Dronabinol
options.C: Ondansetron
options.D: Dexamethasone
options.E: Aprepitant

why: Ondansetron prolongs QT and can cause torsades; congenital long QT syndrome (and apomorphine co-use) are contraindications. A CINV regimen can lean on the NK1 antagonist and dexamethasone instead.

whys.A: Anticholinergic; not a QT contraindication.
whys.D: CINV adjunct; no QT contraindication.
whys.E: NK1 antagonist; its issues are CYP3A4 interactions, not QT contraindication.

takeaway: Ondansetron: QT/torsades — contraindicated in congenital long QT.
discriminator: Know each antiemetic's signature risk: 5-HT3 QT, D2 TD/dystonia, NK1 CYP3A4, CB1 psychoactive.

stem: A patient with Crohn disease takes budesonide 9 mg every morning. He starts ketoconazole for a fungal infection and drinks grapefruit juice daily. Two weeks later he has a round face and high glucose. Why?

options.A: CYP3A4 inhibition raised budesonide's systemic exposure
options.B: Ketoconazole induced cortisol production
options.C: Grapefruit juice blocks budesonide absorption
options.D: Budesonide has no first-pass metabolism
options.E: Expected effect of 9 mg on any regimen

why: Budesonide's high first-pass metabolism (CYP3A4) keeps systemic exposure low. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, grapefruit juice) remove that protection → hypercortisolism.

whys.C: It inhibits CYP3A4, raising exposure.
whys.D: It has high first-pass metabolism — normally.
whys.E: Low systemic exposure is budesonide's advantage.

takeaway: Budesonide + CYP3A4 inhibitor → Cushingoid effects.
discriminator: First-pass metabolism is the safety feature an inhibitor removes (Unit 1).

stem: A 29-year-old on a combined oral contraceptive and warfarin starts a CINV regimen with aprepitant. Which counseling is most accurate?

options.A: No interaction; aprepitant is not metabolized by CYP
options.B: Aprepitant raises the INR, so cut the warfarin dose now
options.C: Aprepitant raises the contraceptive's estrogen level
options.D: Stop warfarin for the 3 days of aprepitant
options.E: Use backup contraception and expect closer INR checks

why: Aprepitant is a CYP3A4 substrate and moderate inhibitor that lowers the effect of warfarin and hormonal contraceptives: use backup contraception and monitor the INR.

whys.A: It is a CYP3A4 substrate and moderate inhibitor.
whys.C: It lowers the contraceptive effect.
whys.D: Monitoring, not stopping, is the response.

takeaway: Aprepitant ↓ warfarin and ↓ hormonal contraceptive effect.
discriminator: Direction matters: here both partner drugs lose effect.

stem: A patient starts bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole). She also takes ferrous sulfate daily and chews calcium carbonate for heartburn. What is the most important counseling point about these extra products?

options.A: Take all of them together to simplify the schedule
options.B: Stop the PPI while taking calcium carbonate
options.C: Switch the iron to IV for the 14-day course
options.D: Space calcium and iron away from tetracycline
options.E: Expect black stools, so stop the iron until done

why: Tetracycline is chelated by dairy, antacids and iron, and calcium carbonate binds tetracyclines, quinolones, levothyroxine and iron. Space them (about 2 hours) so the antibiotic is absorbed.

whys.A: Calcium and iron chelate tetracycline and lower absorption.
whys.B: The PPI is part of the regimen; the problem is chelation of tetracycline.
whys.C: Spacing the doses solves the interaction.
whys.E: Bismuth darkens stools; iron is not the reason to stop.

takeaway: Tetracycline + calcium/iron/antacids/dairy → chelation → separate doses.
discriminator: Chelation lowers antibiotic absorption — a timing fix, not a drug swap.

stem: A 58-year-old with type 2 diabetes and CKD stage 3 has a duodenal ulcer. Sucralfate 1 g four times daily is considered. Which pair of concerns is most relevant to him?

options.A: Pregnancy risk and uterine cramping
options.B: Tardive dyskinesia and acute dystonia
options.C: CYP2C19 inhibition and B12 deficiency
options.D: QT prolongation and serotonin syndrome
options.E: Aluminum accumulation and higher blood glucose

why: Sucralfate contains aluminum that accumulates in CKD, can raise glucose in diabetes, can form bezoars and binds other drugs (separate by 2 hours).

whys.A: Those are misoprostol concerns.
whys.C: Those are PPI concerns.
whys.D: Those are ondansetron concerns.

takeaway: Sucralfate: aluminum (CKD), hyperglycemia (diabetes), bezoar, binds drugs.
discriminator: Match each mucosal agent to its own patient filter: sucralfate = CKD/diabetes; misoprostol = pregnancy.

stem: A patient starting sulfasalazine for ulcerative colitis has G6PD deficiency and a sulfa allergy. What is the best decision?

options.A: Use sulfasalazine with folic acid 1 mg daily
options.B: Avoid sulfasalazine; choose mesalamine instead
options.C: Use sulfasalazine and check a CBC monthly
options.D: Skip 5-ASA therapy and start a biologic
options.E: Use sulfasalazine at half the usual dose

why: Sulfasalazine is contraindicated with sulfa or salicylate allergy and causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency (plus agranulocytosis, SJS, folate deficiency). Mesalamine delivers 5-ASA without the sulfa component.

whys.A: Folic acid prevents folate deficiency, not allergy or hemolysis.
whys.C: Sulfa allergy is a contraindication; G6PD raises hemolysis risk.
whys.D: Mild disease starts with 5-ASA — mesalamine fits.
whys.E: Dose reduction does not remove the contraindication.

takeaway: Sulfa allergy or G6PD → avoid sulfasalazine; mesalamine is the 5-ASA alternative.
discriminator: Same active moiety (5-ASA), different carrier — the carrier carries the sulfa risk.

stem: A patient on warfarin has had stable INRs of 2.5 for a year. Over 3 weeks her INR falls to 1.4 with perfect adherence. She recently started a mood supplement. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.A: St. John's wort induced CYP3A4
options.B: Vitamin K deficiency from the supplement
options.C: St. John's wort inhibited CYP3A4
options.D: Ginkgo biloba increased clotting factor synthesis
options.E: Fish oil lowered warfarin absorption

why: St. John's wort induces CYP3A4, increasing warfarin metabolism and lowering the INR. That is why supplement use is a required part of medication reconciliation.

whys.C: It induces, which lowers the INR.
whys.D: Ginkgo increases bleeding risk.
whys.E: Fish oil adds bleeding risk at high doses.

takeaway: St. John's wort ↓ INR (induction); ginkgo/fish oil ↑ bleeding.
discriminator: Inducer → lower level → less effect (Unit 1).

stem: A patient with cirrhosis takes lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy. He now has 8 watery stools a day, is dizzy, and his sodium is high. What is the best adjustment?

options.A: Keep the dose and add magnesium hydroxide
options.B: Increase lactulose to clear more ammonia
options.C: Reduce it to reach 2–3 soft stools a day
options.D: Stop lactulose and start loperamide
options.E: Switch to senna for gentler stools

why: Lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy is titrated to 2–3 soft stools a day; over-use causes dehydration and hypernatremia.

whys.A: Adds another osmotic laxative.
whys.D: Encephalopathy still needs treatment; titrate instead.
whys.E: Stimulant laxatives don't treat encephalopathy.

takeaway: Lactulose target: 2–3 soft stools/day.
discriminator: The stool count is the dosing gauge.

stem: A 27-year-old needs daily naproxen for 3 months after an NSAID ulcer. She is sexually active and uses no contraception. Which ulcer prophylaxis plan is best?

options.A: Misoprostol 200 mcg four times daily with food
options.B: A daily PPI rather than misoprostol
options.C: Misoprostol now, then a pregnancy test monthly
options.D: Sucralfate taken with the naproxen doses
options.E: No prophylaxis, since the ulcer has healed

why: Misoprostol replaces the prostaglandins NSAIDs remove, but it is a potent uterotonic with a pregnancy boxed warning. With possible pregnancy and no contraception, a PPI protects without that risk.

whys.A: Boxed warning: pregnancy — miscarriage, uterine rupture, birth defects.
whys.C: Testing after exposure does not prevent harm.
whys.D: Sucralfate binds other drugs; not the taught NSAID prophylaxis.
whys.E: A prior NSAID ulcer is the reason to protect.

takeaway: Possible pregnancy + NSAID ulcer prophylaxis → PPI, not misoprostol.
discriminator: The single most important question before misoprostol: could she be pregnant?

stem: A cruise passenger applied a scopolamine patch behind her ear the night before. The next day one pupil is widely dilated, but she has no headache, weakness or confusion. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Acute stroke until proven otherwise
options.B: Patch residue on her fingers touched the eye
options.C: Serotonin syndrome from the anticholinergic
options.D: Withdrawal from removing the patch too soon
options.E: Expected systemic effect of the patch

why: Scopolamine is anticholinergic; touching the patch then the eye dilates that pupil. Counsel: wash hands after handling; apply at least 4 hours before travel, replace every 72 hours; avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma.

whys.A: Isolated dilation after handling a patch, with no deficits, fits contamination.
whys.C: Not a scopolamine effect.
whys.D: Withdrawal causes nausea and dizziness.
whys.E: Systemic effects are bilateral; one pupil suggests local contact.

takeaway: Scopolamine patch: wash hands — one dilated pupil.
discriminator: Unilateral after contact = local anticholinergic effect.

stem: A severely malnourished patient who has barely eaten for 3 weeks is about to start nutrition support. Which plan best prevents refeeding syndrome?

options.A: Give thiamine only after feeding begins
options.B: Check electrolytes weekly once feeding starts
options.C: Start full calories at once to restore weight quickly
options.D: Use IV glucose alone for the first 3 days
options.E: Thiamine first, slow start, daily phosphate/K/Mg

why: Carbohydrate feeding raises insulin, shifting phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells — dangerously low levels with heart, muscle and breathing problems. Feed slowly, monitor daily, give thiamine first.

whys.A: Thiamine is given before feeding.
whys.B: Daily checks are needed at the start.
whys.C: Rapid carbohydrate load drives the dangerous shifts.
whys.D: Carbohydrate drives insulin and the shifts.

takeaway: Refeeding: thiamine first, start low, phosphate/K/Mg daily.
discriminator: Insulin drives the electrolytes into cells.

stem: A patient with confirmed H. pylori has a penicillin allergy, took azithromycin 3 months ago and drinks 2 glasses of wine nightly. Which plan is best?

options.A: Amoxicillin triple therapy; avoid alcohol during therapy
options.B: Bismuth quadruple; no alcohol until 3 days after
options.C: PPI alone for 8 weeks, then retest
options.D: Bismuth quadruple therapy; alcohol is fine after day 7
options.E: Clarithromycin triple therapy; limit wine to one glass

why: Penicillin allergy or recent macrolide exposure → bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole) for 14 days. Metronidazole causes a disulfiram-like reaction: avoid alcohol during and for 3 days after.

whys.A: Penicillin allergy rules out amoxicillin.
whys.C: A PPI alone does not eradicate H. pylori.
whys.D: Metronidazole: no alcohol during and for 3 days after.
whys.E: Recent macrolide exposure raises resistance concern.

takeaway: Allergy or macrolide history → bismuth quadruple; metronidazole = no alcohol + 3 days.
discriminator: The regimen choice and the counseling point are both tested.
src: L05 S23; S25; S61; SG U3-R6; SG U3-S

stem: A 62-year-old smoker with ulcerative colitis and a prior myocardial infarction has failed infliximab. Tofacitinib is proposed. Which concern weighs most heavily?

options.A: Interstitial nephritis requiring creatinine checks
options.B: Tardive dyskinesia with use beyond 12 weeks
options.C: Boxed warnings for MACE and thrombosis
options.D: Gut-selective action limiting its effectiveness
options.E: Hypercortisolism with CYP3A4 inhibitors

why: Tofacitinib (JAK inhibitor) carries boxed warnings for serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and thrombosis — highest stakes in an older smoker with prior MI. It is used after TNF-inhibitor failure.

whys.A: That is mesalamine.
whys.D: That describes vedolizumab.
whys.E: That is budesonide.

takeaway: Tofacitinib: boxed MACE, thrombosis, malignancy, infection.
discriminator: The patient's CV history is the filter.

stem: Four days after finishing clindamycin for a dental abscess, a patient has profuse watery diarrhea and a fever of 38.6 °C. He asks for loperamide. What is the best response?

options.A: Start bismuth subsalicylate and recheck in a week
options.B: Give loperamide 4 mg, then 2 mg after each stool
options.C: Give diphenoxylate/atropine instead
options.D: Avoid it; evaluate for C. difficile first
options.E: Give loperamide plus oral rehydration

why: Recent antibiotics + fever + profuse watery diarrhea suggests C. difficile; antimotility agents (loperamide, diphenoxylate) are avoided because slowing transit can worsen toxin-mediated injury. Treat the cause.

whys.A: Delays evaluation of a likely C. difficile infection.
whys.B: Slowing transit can worsen toxin-mediated colitis.
whys.C: Also contraindicated with C. difficile or infectious diarrhea.
whys.E: Rehydration helps, but antimotility agents are still avoided.

takeaway: Fever, bloody stool or C. difficile → no antimotility agents.
discriminator: The red flags (fever, recent antibiotic) turn a routine request into a contraindication.

stem: An 84-year-old with a creatinine clearance of 28 mL/min takes famotidine 40 mg twice daily. Over a week she becomes confused and agitated. Infection workup is negative. What is the most likely explanation and fix?

options.A: Renal accumulation; lower the famotidine dose
options.B: Hypomagnesemia from H2 blockade; add magnesium hydroxide
options.C: Tolerance to famotidine; double the dose
options.D: Cimetidine-like CYP inhibition; switch to omeprazole
options.E: Rebound acid hypersecretion; add sucralfate

why: Famotidine is renally cleared: reduce the dose when CrCl is below 60 mL/min. Accumulation in CKD causes CNS effects, especially in older adults — a Unit 1 renal-dosing principle applied to a Unit 3 drug.

whys.B: Hypomagnesemia is a long-term PPI risk, and magnesium accumulates in CKD.
whys.C: Raising the dose worsens accumulation.
whys.D: Famotidine has minimal CYP effect; the issue is renal accumulation.
whys.E: Rebound follows stopping a PPI; sucralfate adds aluminum in CKD.

takeaway: H2 blockers: reduce dose when CrCl < 60; confusion in older adults with CKD.
discriminator: Accumulation (renal) vs. interaction (CYP) — famotidine is the renal one.

stem: A 31-year-old in opioid withdrawal has been taking 40 mg of OTC loperamide daily to ease symptoms. He presents with syncope. What is the most important next step?

options.A: Check a stool culture for infection
options.B: Get an ECG for QT prolongation and arrhythmia
options.C: Reassure: loperamide does not reach the brain
options.D: Switch to diphenoxylate/atropine at the same dose
options.E: Give naloxone and discharge if he wakes

why: Loperamide maximum is 16 mg/day Rx (8 mg OTC). High doses cause QT prolongation, torsades and cardiac arrest; CNS depression in overdose may need repeated naloxone.

whys.A: Syncope at this dose points to cardiac toxicity.
whys.C: High doses cause cardiac toxicity and CNS depression.
whys.D: Not a fix; also an opioid with toxicity.
whys.E: Cardiac toxicity needs monitoring; naloxone may need repeating.

takeaway: Loperamide misuse → QT/torsades: get an ECG.
discriminator: Peripheral at normal doses ≠ safe at 5× the maximum.
